From Reach to Recurring

Playbooklowob research

By lowob · 30 July 2026 · 7-minute read · Revenue

Reach is rented; recurring is owned. The move is from traffic-dependent revenue to products people pay for repeatedly, measured by conversion, churn, revenue per subscriber and platform independence. The pressure is measurable: Chartbeat data cited by the Reuters Institute shows Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 publisher sites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, and Pew found people clicked a search result on 8% of visits that showed an AI summary, against 15% without one.

The answer-engine problem

For twenty years the deal was simple. You published, search engines sent people, and you sold the attention. That deal is being rewritten without you.

AI summaries and assistants now answer directly. A reader asks a question, gets a synthesised answer, and often never visits the page that supplied the facts. Pew Research Center tracked 900 US adults' Google searches in March 2025: when an AI summary appeared, users clicked a link inside it on just 1% of visits. Publishers expect worse. The Reuters Institute's 2026 trends survey of 280 media leaders found they expect search traffic to fall by more than 40% over three years, while noting it is unclear how much of the recent fall is due to AI summaries.

Chatbots themselves are still a small route to news. Weekly use for news rose from 7% to 10% in the 2026 Digital News Report, and 42% of chatbot news users said they always or often click through to sources. The exposure today sits mainly in search, where summaries now sit above the links.

Any media business whose revenue depends on search referrals is exposed. Programmatic advertising, affiliate links on evergreen pages, and traffic-based sponsor pricing all sit in the path.

Three responses hold up.

Owned channels. Email, membership, apps and communities are relationships no intermediary can intercept. An audience is not a business covers why owned beats rented. This is the practical reason.

Be the source. Assistants cite original reporting, proprietary data, and clear expert positions. They do not cite the fourth rewrite of a press release. Being cited builds brand and sends some traffic, but the real value is authority that converts to paid. Our piece on how LLMs choose sources covers the mechanics.

Products that do not need traffic. Everything in the rest of this piece.

Subscriptions and memberships

The paid relationship is the core of a recurring media business. It is also where most founders under-invest, because free growth feels better than paid conversion.

The ceiling is real. Across 20 markets where paywalls are common, 17% of people paid for online news in the past year, roughly flat, according to the Reuters Institute. Its 2026 report also found reader revenue gains coming increasingly from price and product mix rather than more subscribers: the share of New York Times subscribers paying only for news access fell from 17% to 12%, as most pay for bundles, and USA Today Co. reported total subscribers down 30% in 2025 while revenue per user rose 27%.

Three decisions drive it: what is behind the wall, how you ask, and what happens after someone pays.

Behind the wall should sit the thing your point of view produces: analysis, access, data, or community. Not the news everyone has. The ask should be specific and tied to a moment of value, not a generic banner. After payment, onboarding and the first renewal matter more than acquisition.

The research on retention supports that order. Northwestern University's Medill researchers analysed about 13 terabytes of subscriber data from three US metro newspapers and found that how often people read was the single biggest predictor of whether they kept paying, ahead of the number of stories or time spent. Habit, not volume, keeps a subscriber.

Membership adds a second layer: belonging, access to people, and influence over what gets made. Community is a job, not a number covers community as a job, and our guide to building a community that lasts covers how members are recruited and kept. Membership is where that job gets paid for.

B2B data, research and sponsorship on quality

Business audiences pay for things that reduce their risk or save them time. A publisher covering a sector sits on exactly that material.

Data products: benchmarks, pricing, deal flow, rankings, directories. Research products: reports, briefings, surveys, advisory calls. Both sell on annual contracts with renewal, and both are priced on usefulness, not on audience size.

Sponsorship changes with the same logic. Stop selling CPM. Sell access to a defined audience with a defined behaviour, and price on that. Buyers are asking for it: the IAB's 2025 creator economy study, a trade-body survey of US ad buyers, found 40% ranked overall return on investment as their top measure for creator campaigns, and listed tools that link activity to business outcomes among their main gaps.

Old sponsorshipQuality sponsorship
Priced per thousand impressionsPriced per campaign against a named audience
Proof is delivery numbersProof is response, leads or renewal
Sold to media buyersSold to marketing and sales leaders
Renewal depends on trafficRenewal depends on results

A sponsor who renews is worth more than three who try once. Build the sales process around renewal from the first conversation. Your first ten sponsors are design partners sets out how.

A sponsor who renews is worth more than three who try once.

Affiliate, commerce and events

Affiliate and commerce work when they match the point of view and are disclosed clearly. Recommending what you would recommend anyway, with a visible note that you earn on it, keeps trust intact. In the US the FTC's guidance is specific: disclose the commission next to the link, and "affiliate link" alone is not adequate. Hiding it loses the trust and the revenue together.

Keep affiliate revenue out of the core forecast if it depends on search traffic. It belongs in the exposed column until it is driven by owned channels.

Events can be the highest-margin line or the most expensive mistake. The difference is the model. Small, repeated, sponsor-backed gatherings with ticketed access tend to work. One large annual event with a cost base set before sponsors sign tends not to. Publishers are leaning in: 54% of the media leaders in the Reuters Institute's trends survey named online and physical events a key revenue focus, behind subscriptions at 76%.

Distribution when the platforms are closed covers distribution when platforms will not carry you. Events are distribution and revenue in one, which is why they deserve a proper plan rather than an experiment. Our piece on events that pay back sets out the business case to write before booking.

Metrics for the move

Stop reporting reach argues for measures that show something happened. Media needs a short set of numbers that show the move from traffic to recurring.

MetricDefinitionWhat it tells you
Share of revenue not dependent on platformsRevenue from owned channels and direct contracts, divided by total revenueWhether the business is yours or the platform's
Paid conversionShare of free audience that becomes paying over a defined periodWhether the paid product is worth the ask
ChurnShare of paying relationships lost per period, by cohortWhether the habit holds after the first renewal
Revenue per subscriberTotal recurring revenue divided by paying relationshipsWhether bundles and price are doing their job
Sponsor renewal rateShare of sponsors who buy againWhether sponsorship is a product or a one-off

Report these monthly. Put the first one at the top. I treat it as the single figure that tells a media founder whether the business is theirs or the platform's. Our explainer on customer churn covers the cohort calculation.

Build it to run without you covers the operating side. In media that means systems for renewal, sponsor reporting and product delivery that do not route through the founder's inbox.

lowob takeaways

  • Label the exposed revenue. Programmatic, evergreen affiliate and traffic-priced sponsorship sit in the path of AI summaries.
  • Build the habit. Reading frequency predicts retention better than reading volume.
  • Sell sponsorship on results. Per campaign, against a named audience, proved by response.
  • Lead with platform independence. Report the share of revenue not dependent on platforms first, every month.
Gateway card

Before the next quarterly plan

  • Traffic-dependent revenue identified and labelled as exposed
  • Owned channel growth tracked separately from platform growth
  • Paid product defined around the point of view, not around general news
  • Sponsorship priced on audience definition and results, not CPM
  • Affiliate and commerce disclosed, and excluded from the core forecast if traffic-driven
  • Five recurring metrics reported monthly, platform independence first

Common questions

How do AI answer engines affect publisher revenue?

AI summaries reduce clicks: Pew found users clicked a search result on 8% of visits with a summary, against 15% without. Revenue tied to search referrals, such as programmatic ads, evergreen affiliate pages and traffic-priced sponsorship, is exposed.

What metrics should a media business track instead of reach?

The share of revenue not dependent on platforms, paid conversion, churn by cohort, revenue per subscriber and sponsor renewal rate, reported monthly with platform independence first.

How should a niche publisher price sponsorships?

Per campaign against a named audience, proven by response, leads or renewal rather than impressions, and sold to marketing and sales leaders rather than media buyers.

What predicts whether a digital subscriber renews?

Habit. Northwestern's Medill research across three US newspapers found reading frequency was the strongest predictor of retention, ahead of stories read or time spent.

Sources and notes

  • Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026: executive summary, June 2026. Online survey across 48 markets; payment figures cover 20 paywall-heavy markets; company figures as reported by the Institute.
  • Reuters Institute, Journalism, media and technology trends and predictions 2026, 12 January 2026. Survey of 280 digital leaders plus Chartbeat traffic data; a strategic sample, not representative.
  • Pew Research Center, Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears, 22 July 2025. Browsing data from 900 US adults in March 2025; consumer searches.
  • Nieman Lab, Researchers crunched 13 TB of local newspaper subscriber data, 5 February 2019. Report on Medill Local News Initiative research at Northwestern University; three US metro titles; older than the other sources.
  • IAB, Creator economy ad spend to reach $37 billion in 2025, 20 November 2025. Trade body study of US ad buyers; sample size not stated in the release.
  • Federal Trade Commission, The FTC's Endorsement Guides: What People Are Asking, last updated July 2025. US regulator staff guidance; not a rule in itself.
  • The sponsorship and metrics tables are lowob's framework.
